metadata.title: Do the Average Level and Dispersion of Socio-Economic Background Measures Explain France's Gap in PISA Scores?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses OECD PISA 2009 results at the country level, constructing country aggregates from student-level ESCS (average and dispersion) and relating them to country-level PISA outcomes (average score, P5, P95, and P95/P5). The analysis is therefore not a student-level regression with explicit complex-survey variance estimation described in the working paper text. The authors report OLS-style specifications with small country samples (N around 32–34), and they do not document the use of PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the estimation. For replication with the OECD PISA microdata, analysts should apply the PISA complex survey design weights when estimating student-level ESCS aggregates and when computing any student-level outcome summaries, but this paper’s reported country-level regressions do not specify a weighting variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are country-level PISA outcomes (average score, P5, P95, and P95/P5) derived from PISA 2009 results, but the working paper does not describe how plausible values (PVs) were combined when computing these country-level statistics. Because the paper does not report a PV-combining rule (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or PV-specific estimation details, the PV handling is treated as a reporting gap rather than a design feature. This omission matters because PISA achievement scores are typically based on PVs, and different PV aggregation approaches can affect standard errors and uncertainty quantification.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper analyzes country-level relationships using PISA 2009 outcomes for OECD countries. The dependent variables are country aggregates computed as the average of PISA scores across reading, mathematics, and science, and distributional statistics (P5, P95, and P95/P5) for each country. ESCS is computed at the student level from OECD’s ESCS components (home possessions, cultural possessions, home educational resources/books, parents’ occupational status, and parents’ education in years of schooling) and then aggregated to the country level as (i) the country average of individual ESCS and (ii) the dispersion (standard deviation) of individual ESCS within each country. The regression sample size varies by specification (N reported as 34 in Table 1 and 32 in some columns of Table 1 and Table 3), implying that some countries are excluded due to missing values for the included macro controls (GDP per capita and education spending measures) and/or due to data availability for the ESCS/PISA aggregates.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PISA 2009 to test whether cross-country differences in students’ socio-economic background (ESCS) explain France’s relative performance. ESCS is computed at the student level from OECD’s ESCS components and then aggregated to each country as the mean ESCS and the dispersion (standard deviation) of ESCS across students. The paper estimates country-level regressions where the dependent variables are the average PISA score (reading, mathematics, science combined), the 5th percentile (P5), the 95th percentile (P95), and the P95/P5 inequality ratio. Results show that ESCS mean and especially ESCS dispersion are strongly associated with country differences in average performance, with ESCS explaining about 60% of the variance in average PISA scores across countries. After adjusting France’s average PISA score for ESCS differences, the France–best-performer gap (Finland, Korea, Japan, Canada) is reduced by about 50%, but not eliminated. The authors caution that endogeneity and the small country sample limit causal interpretation, and the paper does not document how PVs and missing data were handled when constructing PISA distributional statistics.
